evidence_items.claim: Bought with a price is redemption imagery in a slaveholding world; it cannot turn church leaders or spouses into owners of another person's body.
Chapter 7's reciprocity gives spouses mutual claims in an ancient patriarchal setting, but it cannot override consent or excuse marital sexual abuse.
Celibacy and marriage are differentiated gifts; the chapter cannot authorize forced marriage, forced celibacy, or treating single people as incomplete.
Divorce counsel addresses ancient cases but must not coerce someone to remain with an abusive spouse or prevent safety, legal help, and pastoral care.
Unbelieving spouse language cannot justify contempt, forced conversion, unequal citizenship, or treating children of mixed households as contaminated.
Remain in the calling is pastoral counsel within present conditions, not a universal ban on emancipation, social mobility, education, or changing harmful work.
The text addresses slavery inside a slave society but cannot justify enslavement, trafficking, worker exploitation, or romanticizing obedience under coercion.
Whether use it rather refers to freedom or slavery is grammatically disputed; certainty about Paul's emancipation advice should remain limited.
Parthenoi may designate virgins, betrothed women, or engaged people; translations should disclose rather than conceal the uncertainty.
Present distress and shortened time shape the counsel; crisis language should not be made into permanent control over another person's vocation.
The Corinthians' letter is lost; quotation marks around proposed slogans reconstruct dialogue and are not manuscript punctuation.
P15, P46, P123, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, and Claromontanus preserve different portions and variants; no one witness simply equals the autograph.
Partition theories and local interpolation proposals should be evaluated passage by passage; neither abrupt transitions nor theological preference alone proves excision.
Paul addresses divorce and mixed marriages without resolving every modern legal or safety circumstance.
The extant letter is best treated as a coherent rhetorical whole while local interpolation and partition proposals remain reviewable.
The Corinthians had written Paul about matters addressed from chapter 7 onward.
P15, P46, P123 and the major codices provide material evidence for transmission, variation, and early collection context.
Chapter 7 gives reciprocal marital counsel and also values celibate singleness.
Chapter 7 addresses enslaved people within an accepted institution but does not morally validate slavery.
The identity of the parthenoi in 7:25-38 as virgins, betrothed women, or engaged couples remains disputed.

Galatians, First Corinthians, and Philippians address ancient circumcision, reversal, rivalry, and embodied status; modern intersex surgery and clinical consent questions are not their direct subject.
